# HTTP 301 vs 308: both permanent, but only 308 keeps the method

## What each code means

Both codes mean the same thing: the resource has moved for good. RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics) defines both with the same sentence: the target resource "has been assigned a new permanent URI and any future references to this resource ought to use one of the enclosed URIs" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html). MDN describes both as a permanent move to the URL in the `Location` header (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/301, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/308). The only real difference is how the client must re-send the request.

## How the client treats the method and body

**General rule.** RFC 9110 says that when following a redirect, the user agent re-sends the original request. It changes the method only "according to the redirecting status code's semantics, if applicable." If the method has been changed to GET or HEAD, it removes content-specific header fields such as Content-Type and Content-Length. In practice that means the body is dropped (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html).

**301.** "For historical reasons, a user agent MAY change the request method from POST to GET for the subsequent request" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html).
- RFC 9110 explains the history. HTTP/1.0 meant 301 and 302 to keep the method, but browsers converged on switching to GET.
- So 301 and 302 "have been adjusted to allow a POST request to be redirected as GET."
- RFC 7231, the previous spec, said the same. It made this rewriting conformant because most user agents did it (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7231.html).
- MDN's 301 page says the Fetch Standard uses GET after a 301 response to a POST, "as permitted by the HTTP specification" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/301).
- Result: a POST that gets a 301 may be re-sent as a GET with no body.

**308.** The client must keep both the method and the body.
- RFC 9110 says 307 and 308 were added "to unambiguously indicate method-preserving redirects" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html).
- RFC 7538 says 308 is like 301 "except that it does not allow changing the request method from POST to GET" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7538.html).
- MDN says the method and body "will not be modified by the client in the redirected request" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/308).
- One gap: RFC 9110's own 308 section (15.4.9) does not state the method rule outright. It is implied by the 15.4 introduction and by the 301 section, which points to 308 for cases where the method change is unwanted.

**A source conflict.** MDN's 308 page says that "A 301 Moved Permanently requires the request method and the body to remain unchanged," and calls switching to GET something "incorrectly handled by older clients" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/308). This contradicts:
- RFC 9110 and RFC 7231, which both explicitly allow POST to become GET on a 301.
- MDN's own 301 page.

The RFC text is the normative spec, so the MDN 308 page's statement about 301 should be treated as inaccurate.

**Compatibility note.** 308 is "much younger (June 2014) than its sibling codes and thus might not be recognized everywhere" (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html). RFC 7538 warns that servers cannot rely on automatic redirection by clients that don't recognize 308 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7538.html).

## Cacheability

Both codes are cacheable by default. The wording has changed between spec versions:
- **RFC 9110** calls both "heuristically cacheable" unless the method definition or explicit cache controls say otherwise. Its section 15.1 lists 301 and 308 among the heuristically cacheable codes (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html).
- **Older specs** said "cacheable by default": RFC 7231 for 301 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7231.html) and RFC 7538 for 308 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7538.html).
- **MDN** does not address default cacheability on either page.

## Where each is specified

**Today.** Both codes are defined in RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics: 301 in section 15.4.2 and 308 in section 15.4.9 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html). MDN also cites "HTTP Semantics" for both.

**History.**
- **301:** Previously defined in RFC 7231 §6.4.2, published in June 2014, which obsoleted RFC 2616 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7231.html).
- **308:** First defined in the Experimental RFC 7238. It was then re-published with "no technical changes" as Standards Track RFC 7538 in April 2015 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7538.html). RFC 9110 cites RFC 7538 as the origin of 308.

**Not verified.**
- Neither of the rfc-editor pages that were opened (RFC 7231 and RFC 7538) showed an "Obsoleted by RFC 9110" line. So I can't confirm from a retrieved source that they are formally obsoleted.
- The IANA HTTP Status Code Registry returned 404 at every URL tried, so its current references for 301 and 308 were not checked.
